extracted.intended_audience: readers of 19th-century travel / colonial exploration accounts; colonial officials, settlers, and surveyors
extracted.subtask_description: First-person 19th-century travelogue / exploration report describing coasts, surveys, country suitability for settlement, and ethnographic encounters. Emphasizes measured observations, practical judgments about land/harbour suitability, and descriptive detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement suitability — three necessary articles
rubrics_metrics.description: "this part of the country was not fit for the settler, being deficient in the three most necessary articles, water, timber for building, and food for stock."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence/absence of water, building timber, and fodder for stock as primary, decisive criteria when judging whether a district is fit for large-scale settlement; absence implies sterility, likely loss to settlers, and risk to life and property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exaggerated or false representations to settlers
rubrics_metrics.description: Author's moral/evaluative stance: it is regrettable for energetic agents to be "totally abandoned by those who sent him out" and to induce people by "false, or at least exaggerated representations" to emigrate to sterile country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports and promotional accounts should not overstate capabilities of country; honesty and careful verification are ethical obligations because people's lives and property depend on such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-hand observation over distant conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Mr. Moore: he "judged entirely from a distant view with the naked eye" and his testimony was "much too vague to justify the expression of any decided opinion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct, on-the-ground examination (digging for water, crossing country) and measured observations to distant, unaided viewing; be cautious about drawing firm conclusions from distant or cursory sightings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harbour / anchorage evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether there is "good anchorage" and shelter; note soundings, reefs, sandbanks, entrance visibility, and exposure to gales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record depths (fathoms), presence and position of reefs and sandbanks, how the mouth behaves in gales, and whether natural features provide shelter from prevailing winds. Example: excepting Champion Bay, there was "no good anchorage on the coast between the latitudes of 28 degrees 20 minutes South and 29 degrees 20 minutes South."

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey and chart accuracy — verify map positions
rubrics_metrics.description: The author repeatedly verifies and corrects chart positions (e.g., "laid down four miles too much to the northward") and compares bearings to detect errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate published charts by taking bearings to known peaks, meridian distances, and other observations; when discrepancies appear (latitude/longitude errors), document them and, if possible, correct the charts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of proper surveying instruments and quantitative measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent use of instruments and measurements: barometric measurement for elevation, compass bearings, soundings in fathoms, latitudes and longitudes, meridian distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support narrative claims with precise numerical observations (elevations in feet, bearings, lat/long, soundings). Examples: Mount Fairfax 582 feet, Wizard Peak 715 feet, soundings of 7 and 12 fathoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soil and vegetation assessment for agricultural potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the soil (sandy, alluvial, ironstone gravel) and accompanying vegetation (stunted gum, banksia, warran) to judge fertility and pastoral potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note soil types and their distribution (surface humus vs deep sand), presence of alluvial deposits, and species indicative of fertility (e.g., warran/yam in valleys). Example guidance: deeper holes dug by natives revealed "the more pure was the sand; it was only the surface soil that held decayed vegetable matter."

rubrics_metrics.name: Railroad/transport feasibility criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for converting a road to a railroad: "there is sufficient width for a single line of rails without detracting from its present value"; level terrain and expected traffic/profitability due to increasing exports/imports and mineral resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing a railroad, ensure adequate right-of-way width, favorable gradients/level ground, and a plausible traffic base (exports/imports, mineral development) to justify profitability; consider connections (e.g., between outer discharge points and the port).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harbour engineering / safety considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical notes on harbour safety: wrecks indicate exposure; a breakwater might remedy exposure; estuary channels and reef foundations affect potential improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a bay for improvement, note existing wrecks and reef alignments, potential natural foundations for breakwaters, tidal outlets that relieve strain on cables during rainy seasons, and where a breakwater could protect harbor anchorage (example: Point Casuarina).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnographic and natural-history observation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Record indigenous practices and natural details with specificity (e.g., native fishing method using nets and coordination; description of a native grave and its ornaments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed descriptions of observed cultural practices, burial forms, and native material culture; include method, equipment, and social context rather than vague or merely anecdotal mentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive travel-writing practice — combine sensory detail with precision
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative couples vivid landscape description with precise bearings, distances, and technical detail (e.g., "the road leading along the foot of a hill covered with wood... glimpse of the beautiful estuary... surface just ruffled and glittering").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good travel/report writing blends evocative sensory details (scenery, weather, colors) with concrete, verifiable facts (distances, compass points, heights). This combination strengthens readability and credibility.
